--- ## title: "Converted Presentation" format: revealjs: theme: default pagetitle: 'Age-structured population models' slide-number: true lang: en --- # Introduction {visibility="hidden"} ## {content-align="center" style="font-size: 160%;"}
**Age-structured and stage-structured
population models**
![](figs/AMRE-HY-male.PNG){height="7cm"} ![](figs/AMRE-SY-male.jpg){height="7cm"} ![](figs/AMRE-ASY-M.jpg){height="7cm"}
## Motivation
::: {style='font-size: 90%;'} Birth and death rates usually depend on age.
::: {.fragment} Growth rates will differ between populations with different age structures. :::
::: {.fragment} Some age classes contribute more to population growth than others. :::
::: {.fragment} These facts have important management implications. ::: ::: ## Human mortality risk
![](figs/Mortality_by_age.png){height="15cm"}
## Human age distributions ::: {style='font-size: 70%;'} **Declining populations have relatively more old individuals than growing populations.** :::
![](figs/AgeStructures.png)
## Three age class example ::: {style='font-size: 70%;'} Abundance of age class $i$ in year $t$ is denoted by $n_{i,t}$. ::: {.fragment} The model for $n_{i,t+1}$ depends on: - Age class survival $s_{i}$, and - Age class fecundity $f_{i}$ - Fecundity is the birth rate ($b_i$) multiplied by survival * In pre-reproductive surveys, $f_i = b_i \times s_0$ * In post-reproductive surveys, $f_i = b_i \times s_i$ ::: ::: ::: {.fragment}
![](figs/age-diagram.png){width="50%"}
```{mermaid} %%| label: "age-diagram" %%| fig-align: "center" %%| fig-width: 5 --- config: flowchart: nodeSpacing: 50 rankSpacing: 50 padding: 15 theme: forest layout: elk elk: nodePlacementStrategy: LINEAR_SEGMENTS nodePlacementAlignment: NONE --- flowchart LR n1(("$$n_{1,t}$$")) --> n2(("$$n_{2,t}$$")) --> n3(("$$n_{3,t}$$")) n2 --> n1 n3 --> n1 ``` ::: ## How does this population grow? ::: {style='font-size: 80%;'} Age class | Equation -------------- | --------------------------------------------------- 1 | $n_{1,t+1} = n_{1,t} \times f_1 + n_{2,t} \times f_2 + n_{3,t} \times f_3$ 2 | $n_{2,t+1} = n_{1,t} \times s_{1}$ 3 | $n_{3,t+1} = n_{2,t} \times s_{2}$
::: {.fragment} According to this particular age-structured model, all animals die after spending one time interval in the third age class. :::
::: {.fragment} In stage-structured models, animals can stay in a class for more than one time interval. ::: ::: ## [Age-class abundance and age distribution]{style="font-size: 90%;"} ::: {style='font-size: 80%;'} - Suppose initial abundance in the 3 age classes is: * $n_{1,1} = 50$ (Age class 1, juveniles) * $n_{2,1} = 40$ (Age class 2, subadults) * $n_{3,1} = 10$ (Age class 3, adults) * $N_1$ = 100 ::: {.fragment} - This implies an initial age distribution of: * $c_{1,1} = n_{1,1}/N_1 = 0.5$ * $c_{2,1} = n_{2,1}/N_1 = 0.4$ * $c_{3,1} = n_{3,1}/N_1 = 0.1$ ::: ::: {.fragment}
**An age distribution describes the proportion of individuals in each age class**
::: ::: ## Age distribution ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](lecture-age-structure_files/figure-revealjs/struc1-1.png){fig-align='center' width=95%} ::: ::: ## Example
Let's choose values of $s_i$ and $f_i$

::: {style='font-size: 80%;'} ----------- ------------------------- ---------------------- ---------------- Age class Initial population size Survival probability Fecundity rate $n_{i,1}$ $s_i$ $f_i$ 1 50 0.5 0.0 2 40 0.6 0.8 3 10 0.0 1.7 ----------- ------------------------- ---------------------- ---------------- ::: ## Population size, *n~i,t~* ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](lecture-age-structure_files/figure-revealjs/proj1-1.png){fig-align='center' width=100%} ::: ::: ## Growth rates, *lambda~i,t~=n~i,t~/n~i,t-1~* ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](lecture-age-structure_files/figure-revealjs/lambda1-1.png){fig-align='center' width=90%} ::: ::: ## Age distribution, *c~i,t~=n~i,t~/N~t~* ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](lecture-age-structure_files/figure-revealjs/prop1-1.png){fig-align='center' width=100%} ::: ::: ## Important things to note ::: {style='font-size: 75%;'} Age distribution converges to a **stable age distribution** when survival and fecundity rates are constant.
::: {.fragment} Stable age distribution is the proportion of individuals in each age class when the population converges. :::
::: {.fragment} Growth rates of each age class differ at first, but converge once the stable age distribution is reached. :::
::: {.fragment} Asymptotic growth rate is $\lambda$ (without subscript). :::
::: {.fragment} Growth rate at the stable age distribution is the same for all age classes, and it is geometric! ::: ::: # Matrix Models ## Matrix models Matrix models aren't actually *new* models.
They are the same models we have been talking about.
::: {.fragment} But, they make it much easier to compute important quantities like $\lambda$ and *reproductive value*. ::: ## Matrix models vs life tables ::: {style='font-size: 75%;'} ::: {.columns} ::: {.column width="50%"} **Matrix models** - Age is discrete - Age class is denoted by $i$ - Each age class can have its own vital rates ::: ::: {.column width="50%"} **Life tables** - Age is continuous - Actual age is denoted by $x$ - Each age can have its own vital rates ::: ::: :::
![](figs/age-class-diagram){width="70%"}
## What is a matrix? ::: {style='font-size: 80%;'} **Definition**: A matrix is a rectangular array of numbers - Usually denoted by an uppercase, bold letter - Either square or rounded brackets are used - Usually, rows are indexed by $i$, columns by $j$ Example of a $3 \times 4$ matrix: \par $$ { \bf A} = \begin{bmatrix} a_{1,1} & a_{1,2} & a_{1,3} & a_{1,4} \\ a_{2,1} & a_{2,2} & a_{2,3} & a_{2,4} \\ a_{3,1} & a_{3,2} & a_{3,3} & a_{3,4} \end{bmatrix} $$ ::: ## Leslie matrix ::: {style='font-size: 80%;'} **What is it?** - Square matrix - Fecundities on first row - Survival probs on lower off-diagonal Example:
$$ {\bf A} = \begin{bmatrix} f_1 & f_2 & f_3 & f_4 \\ s_1 & 0 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & s_2 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & s_3 & 0 \end{bmatrix} $$
::: ## How do we use a Leslie matrix? ::: {style='font-size: 80%;'} These two expressions are equivalent: Age class | Equation -------------- | ------------------------------------------------------- 1 | $n_{1,t+1} = n_{1,t} \times f_{1} + n_{2,t} \times f_{2} + n_{3,t} \times f_3$ 2 | $n_{2,t+1} = n_{1,t} \times s_{1}$ 3 | $n_{3,t+1} = n_{2,t} \times s_{2}$ AND $${\bf n}_{t+1} = {\bf A}\times {\bf n}_{t}$$ ::: ## Matrix multiplication
$$ \begin{bmatrix} aw + bx + cy + dz \\ ew + fx + gy + hz \\ iw + jx + ky + lz \\ mw + nx + oy + pz \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} a & b & c & d \\ e & f & g & h \\ i & j & k & l \\ m & n & o & p \end{bmatrix} \times \begin{bmatrix} w \\ x \\ y \\ z \end{bmatrix} $$ ## [Matrix multiplication and Leslie matrix]{style="font-size: 90%;"} $$ \begin{bmatrix} n_{1,t+1} \\ n_{2,t+1} \\ n_{3,t+1} \\ n_{4,t+1} \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} f_1 & f_2 & f_3 & f_4 \\ s_1 & 0 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & s_2 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & s_3 & 0 \end{bmatrix} \times \begin{bmatrix} n_{1,t} \\ n_{2,t} \\ n_{3,t} \\ n_{4,t} \end{bmatrix} $$ # Reproductive value ## Reproductive Value ::: {style='font-size: 80%;'} **Definition**: The extent to which an individual in age class $i$ will contribute to the ancestry of future generations. $$ v_i = \sum_{j=i}^{I}\left(\prod_{h=i}^{j-1}s_h\right)f_j\lambda^{i-j-1} $$
::: {.fragment} Post-reproductive individuals have reproductive values of zero. :::
::: {.fragment} Depending on survival and fecundity rates, a first-year individual could have a higher or lower reproductive value than a second-year individual. ::: ::: ## [Reproductive value for previous example]{style="font-size: 80%;"} ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](lecture-age-structure_files/figure-revealjs/rv-1.png){fig-align='center' width=90%} ::: ::: ## Other important quantities ::: {style='font-size: 80%;'} **Net reproductive rate** The expected number of individuals produced by an individual over its lifetime: $$ R_0 = \sum_{i=1}^I \left(\prod_{j=1}^{i-1} s_j\right)f_i $$ ::: {.fragment} **Generation time** The time required for a population to increase by a factor of $R_0$. $$ T = \frac{\log(R_0)}{\log(\lambda)} $$ ::: ::: ## Other properties of the Leslie matrix The dominant eigenvalue of ${\bf A}$ is the growth rate $\lambda$.
The right eigenvector gives the **stable age distribution**.
The left eigenvector gives the **reproductive value**. # Stage-structured models ## Stage-structured population models ::: {style='font-size: 80%;'} Age isn't always the best way to think about population structure. ::: {.fragment} For some populations, it is much more useful to think about size structure or even spatial structure. ::: ::: {.fragment} These "stage-structured" models differ from age-structured models in that individuals can remain in a stage class (with probability $1-p_i$) for multiple time periods. ::: ::: ::: {.fragment}
![](figs/stage-diagram.png){width="70%"}
::: ## Stage-structured population models ::: {.fragment} In stage-structured models, individuals transition from one stage to the next with probability $p_i$. ::: {.fragment} We can add these transition probabilities to our projection matrix like this: $$ {\bf A} = \begin{bmatrix} f_1 & f_2 & f_3 \\ s_1 & s_2(1-p_2) & 0 \\ 0 & s_2 p_2 & s_3 \end{bmatrix} $$ ::: ::: {.fragment} This example allows for individual to remain in stages 2 and 3 for more than one time period. ::: ::: ## Summary ::: {style='font-size: 80%;'} Vital rates ($s$ and $f$) are usually age-specific.
::: {.fragment} Population growth will depend on age distribution. :::
::: {.fragment} If vital rates are constant, population will reach stable age distribution with constant growth rate $\lambda$. :::
::: {.fragment} Reproductive value indicates which age class contributes the most to population growth. :::
::: {.fragment} Matrix models are a convenient method used to work with age-structured populations. ::: :::

<script>
  // htmlwidgets need to know to resize themselves when slides are shown/hidden.
  // Fire the "slideenter" event (handled by htmlwidgets.js) when the current
  // slide changes (different for each slide format).
  (function () {
    // dispatch for htmlwidgets
    function fireSlideEnter() {
      const event = window.document.createEvent("Event");
      event.initEvent("slideenter", true, true);
      window.document.dispatchEvent(event);
    }

    function fireSlideChanged(previousSlide, currentSlide) {
      fireSlideEnter();

      // dispatch for shiny
      if (window.jQuery) {
        if (previousSlide) {
          window.jQuery(previousSlide).trigger("hidden");
        }
        if (currentSlide) {
          window.jQuery(currentSlide).trigger("shown");
        }
      }
    }

    // hookup for slidy
    if (window.w3c_slidy) {
      window.w3c_slidy.add_observer(function (slide_num) {
        // slide_num starts at position 1
        fireSlideChanged(null, w3c_slidy.slides[slide_num - 1]);
      });
    }

  })();
</script>
